outline.title: Durability and the write path
outline.subtitle: When the database says "committed", what exactly has happened on disk — and what can a crash one millisecond later still lose?
outline.assumes: page cache and fsync cost (1.5), honest measurement (1.1)
outline.introduces: write-ahead log, fsync semantics and what it does not guarantee, torn and partial writes, checksums, checkpoint, crash recovery and replay, the durability boundary, group commit
outline.leavesForLater: replication and what a replica has (5.3), storage structures on top of the log (4.2)
sections: 1.6 — Group commit and the durability–throughput trade

outline.title: Storage structures
outline.subtitle: Why does the same workload run ten times faster on one storage structure than another, and how do you tell which one you need before you have built the wrong one?
outline.assumes: the write-ahead log (4.1), the page cache (1.5)
outline.introduces: pages and the buffer pool, B-tree, LSM tree, compaction, Bloom filter, read/write/space amplification, matching structure to workload, cache eviction policies (LRU, LFU, 2Q, ARC)
outline.leavesForLater: indexes as the planner sees them (4.4), partitioning (4.4)

outline.title: Transactions and concurrency control
outline.subtitle: Two transactions both read, both write, both commit without error — and the result is one neither of them would have produced alone. Which isolation level allowed that, and which would have stopped it?
outline.assumes: the write path (4.1), concurrency correctness on one process (1.4)
outline.introduces: atomicity, isolation levels, MVCC and snapshots, lost update, write skew, phantom reads, locks and deadlocks, snapshot isolation vs serializable, optimistic vs pessimistic concurrency, serialization failures and retry, the transactional outbox as a same-transaction write

outline.title: Query planning and production evolution
outline.subtitle: Why did the planner choose a sequential scan over your index, and what will your migration do to the table while it runs?
outline.introduces: EXPLAIN and EXPLAIN ANALYZE, cardinality estimation and statistics, access paths and index selectivity, join strategies, vacuum and bloat, table partitioning, migration locks, expand/contract schema changes, rollback and compatibility
outline.leavesForLater: safe change as a release discipline (6.3), schema evolution across services (7.2)

commitments.text: What fsync promises about durability, beyond its latency, belongs to a later course (elite-performance course.json, deferred). Storage section 1.3 pays it.
commitments.resolution: Section 1.3: plain fsync hands data to the drive; on macOS the drive may keep it in its volatile cache, and Apple's fsync(2) says an OS crash or power loss may lose some or none of it; F_FULLFSYNC asks the drive to flush. Linux fsync on ext4 sends the flush command; after an fsync error Linux marks pages clean (Rebello et al. 2020), so PostgreSQL PANICs since 2019-02-14.

2.2: a PostgreSQL table is a heap with line pointers and every index points at a TID; InnoDB rows live in the clustered primary-key B-tree. TOAST, nbtree deduplication (13), bottom-up deletion (14), HOT counters.
Write model counts the heap page and one leaf per index, each with its own full-page image (Vondra 2016: about 2 GB WAL with BIGSERIAL vs over 40 GB with UUID).

2.7: MyRocks reads by primary key before writes; an LSM update writes the whole row (about 406 MB/s at 10,000 updates/s of 1,230-byte rows and write amplification 33), so the first draft's '5 to 15 times fewer bytes' was wrong and is corrected.

2.8: the scan ring protects only sequential scans; 2.1: PostgreSQL reads can be OS page-cache hits; 2.4: tombstones under range scans, real RocksDB stall log format (column_family.cc v11.8.1), Compaction Stats; new E13 with pageinspect, pgstatindex, pg_stat_wal.

The failsafe is not the aggressive freezing scan: it drops the cost-based delay and skips index vacuuming (vacuum_failsafe_age, PG 14 docs).
The forced Index Scan at random_page_cost 1.0 costs 17,319.42, not 48,276 (its cost at 4.0); cost_model.py --sweep agrees.

fixed: Tiered (universal) compaction space made consistent: old versions can reach up to 3 times the data by default (max_size_amplification_percent 200, universal_compaction.h v11.8.1 lines 45-48 and 137) before a full compaction; a merge needs temporary room for its output, up to 2 times the files it rewrites (Universal Compaction wiki).
